lines.note: Continues the preceding entry: ugatsu nioi de gozaru describes a piercing smell. The Portuguese begins its explanation as a smell that seems to strip the nose.
Completes the pungent-smell comparison: it seems to flay the nostrils. This is the continuation of the preceding Japanese example, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Saber letras, ou ter eſtudado. Vt,

lines.note: Ugaku denotes learning or literacy, explained as knowing letters or having studied. The printed final o in eſtudado corrects OCR eſtudade; V- starts the contrasted example below.

runs.text: O q̃ tem eſtudado, & não tem

lines.note: V-gacu and mugacu contrast the learned and the unlearned. The abbreviated q̃ is retained rather than expanded, and the Portuguese contrast continues onto the next row.

runs.text: eſtudado, ou o q̃ ſabe letras, & o q̃ não ſabe.

lines.note: Completes the contrast between someone who has studied and someone who has not, equivalently someone who knows letters and someone who does not.
Ugai wo suru means rinsing the mouth. The headword and its verbal example agree directly with the Portuguese gloss.
Chozu ugai shite combines washing the hands with rinsing the mouth. The scan has capital Vt and a caron in Chǒzzu; the Portuguese coordination continues below.
Adds the mouth to the preceding washing of the hands. The article a and noun boca are visibly separated, correcting OCR aboca.

runs.text: Bacia, ou gamela de pao pera la-

lines.note: Ugaidarai is a basin for rinsing the mouth, described as a basin or wooden bowl. The Portuguese verb begins la- and continues on the next physical row.
Completes la-uar a boca, washing or rinsing the mouth, and therefore defines the purpose of the preceding basin.
Uji, alternatively sujime, is family origin or lineage. The upright l is the alternative marker, and the Portuguese li- continues as linha.
Completes linha da geracao, the line of descent. The printed accent in gèração is retained rather than modernizing the historical spelling.
Ujisho is referred back to the preceding family-origin or lineage definition. The caron over the final vowel is visible in the scan.
Ujishujo receives the same lineage or family-origin meaning. Its separate physical entry and final caron are retained.
Ugo is explained by ame no nochi, after rain, and the Portuguese agrees: after it has rained. Historical chouer is preserved.

Ugokashi / ugokasu means to move or cause something to stir. The expected past-form string is aita, also supplied by the attributed NINJAL headword index, but this impression leaves a blank between ai and a; the visible ai a is preserved without inventing a t. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The scan remains the transcription authority.
Completes the transitive definition, making something move. Toki no koe tenchi wo begins the example of a battle cry shaking heaven and earth; the verb continues after v-.

runs.text: A grita dos ſoldados parece que a-

lines.note: Completes ugokasu in the battle-cry example. The Portuguese explains that the soldiers' shouting seemed to shake heaven and earth, with a- continuing below.
Completes abalaua o ceo, & terra. The next Japanese example begins kokoro wo ugokasu, moving someone's heart.

runs.text: Mouer o coração como com perſua-

lines.note: Completes kokoro wo ugokasu and glosses it as moving the heart through persuasion. The scan supports como com, not the garbled OCR cemno com; perſua- continues below.

Sões completes persuasions in the preceding definition. The physically displaced uemente at the right completes le- in the following Vgomeqi gloss; it remains on this observed row with its opening relocation mark. Two overlapping OCR rows have been consolidated here without losing either fragment.

Ugomeki / ugomeku means to stir or wriggle; the gloss is moving gently, with le- completed by displaced uemente above. Reinspection of the damaged middle m, followed by the attributed NINJAL index, supports Vgomeqi rather than OCR Vgoneqi.
Ugoki / ugoku is the intransitive act of moving or being shaken. It contrasts with the earlier causative or transitive Vgocaxi entry.
Ugoki hataraki combines moving with working or acting. The Portuguese begins acting while in motion; the visible e in Mouendoſe corrects OCR Mouendeſe.
Completes the active-work definition as doing something and working. The two coordinated glosses explain the compound rather than introducing another headword.
Ugokiwatari is movement throughout an area. The Portuguese starts a description of shaking in all parts, illustrated by an earthquake on the next lines.

runs.text: as partes, como a terra com algum terremoto

lines.note: Explains the widespread shaking by comparison with the earth during an earthquake. The adjective qualifying that earthquake follows on the next physical row.
Grande completes the preceding earthquake comparison: a great earthquake. This short continuation belongs to Vgoqivatari.
Uge / uguru concerns skin or a crust coming off. The scan clearly supports Esfolarſe, peeling or being stripped, rather than the OCR Fuſcilarſe; co- begins the word for crust.

runs.text: dea como de bustella, ou ſarna. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the crust comparison, as from a scab or skin disease. Casa- begins kasa ga ugueta below; historical bustella is retained.
Completes kasa ga ugueta, a scab coming off. Kishi ga ugueta applies the same verb to a bank collapsing; its Portuguese translation begins Arrui-.

runs.text: nou, ou cahio a terra alta, barroca, &c.

lines.note: Completes arruinou and explains that the high ground or bank fell away. The letter in cahio is h, not OCR b, and alta is supported by the scan and the bank context.
Ugen is possession of miraculous efficacy. The next phrase begins ugen chitoku no so, describing a religious person with such powers.

Completes the phrase for a religious person endowed with efficacy, wisdom and virtue. The Portuguese begins listing many virtues, with virtu- continued below. A separate enlarged second-pass check establishes the circumflex in ſô rather than the OCR caron.
Completes the list as virtues, miracles and learning. The scan reads ſciencia, not the OCR fetencia; this fits chitoku in the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: Vgu i, gǔ, ǔta. l, iboi, ô, ôta.

lines.note: Ugui / uguu and alternative iboi describe the working or maturation of a cauterized sore. The unusual spaced Vgu i is visible and is also retained in the attributed NINJAL index; the carons on u and circumflexes on o remain distinct.

runs.text: o botão de fogo, ou amadurecer, & fazer

lines.note: Explains the action of a cautery and the ripening of a sore. Fazer continues into materia below, referring to the production of discharge.

Materia completes the preceding explanation of a sore producing discharge. The displaced ao roxinol belongs semantically to the following bird comparison but is printed at this row's right edge; the duplicate OCR materia row has been removed without losing text.
Uguisu is described as a small bird resembling a nightingale; the comparison is completed by displaced ao roxinol on the preceding row. The visibly spaced headword is preserved.

The poetic sleeve expression is followed by Vaqiaqeno ſede. Context and the preceding ſode suggest intended sode, but the worn final vowel has an e-like internal stroke; ſede is therefore retained with this caveat. The next lines explain sleeves open at the sides.

runs.text: Mãgas que tem hũas aberturas como as dos

lines.note: Defines sleeves with openings like those of small children's clothing. The visible nasal sign in hũas corrects OCR has.
Completes the comparison with the quimoes of small boys. Quimões is the Portuguese garment word as printed, not a separately embedded Japanese headword.
Uguramochi is a name for the mole, directly glossed by Portuguese toupeira. No modern zoological species is imposed.
Uguromochi is another mole-name with the same meaning. It is aligned as a new headword, so the OCR indentation is removed; the damaged letter sequence supports Vguromochi rather than Vqjuromochi.
Ui suru is explained as putting something under ashes, as a preparation for treatment. The scan supports Viſuru rather than vſſuru, and bai- continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: xo da cinza como mezinha ẽburulhada em pa-

lines.note: Completes debaixo da cinza: medicine wrapped in paper is placed under ashes. The historical nasal abbreviation and spelling ẽburulhada are preserved; pa- continues as papel at the top of column 2.

runs.text: pel molhado pera ſe aquentar, ou lhe tirar algũa

lines.note: Completes pa-pel molhado from column 1: wet paper allows the medicine to warm or lose an undesirable quality. The small word is lhe, not OCR he.
Reima completes the explanation of removing a harmful or acrid quality. Kusuri wo ui suru is the Japanese example applying the preparation to medicine.
Ui describes something miserable or sad. The scan prints an internal hyphen in V-i; the following ui mujo example continues onto the next row.

Completes mujo and explains misery, sadness and the uncertainty of the world. The caron in jǒ and the nasal abbreviation in mũ- are preserved; the compact terminal hyphen is visible next to the right rule.
Completes mundo and adds life: the gloss concerns the uncertainty of the world and of life.

The scan prints the very short V. entry with the adverb label and Vſa. The form is anomalous in relation to the preceding ui adjective; it is retained as printed rather than expanded to a conjectural V-u. The attributed NINJAL index independently records the same short headword.

runs.text: Aprimeira vez que os moços fi-

lines.note: Uikamuri describes a boy's first ceremonial headgear. The printed internal hyphen distinguishes the vowel sequence; fi- begins filhos in the explanation of noble children.

runs.text: lhos de Cũgues mudão o nome, & poem hua

lines.note: Completes filhos: children of kuge nobles change their names and put on special headgear. The d of mudão is badly abraded but its remaining upper stroke and the naming context support the reading; Cũgues is the embedded Japanese social term.
Completes the coming-of-age description as putting a particular cap on the head. The noun belongs to the Portuguese gloss, not a new Japanese item.

runs.text: Aprimeira vez que o minino ſetem

lines.note: Uidachi is a first standing or first going out. The initial illustration is a child standing for the first time, with em pe continued below; the scan supports V-idachi rather than Vnidachi.

runs.text: em pè, ou começa a ãdar. Ite, Aprimeira vez

lines.note: Completes the child's first standing or beginning to walk. Ite introduces another first occasion, explained on the following row.

runs.text: que o doente ſe aleuanta da cama, ou ſae de ca

lines.note: The next application is a sick person first rising from bed or leaving the house. The e in doente is abraded; the surviving letters and context support the word rather than the OCR split do nte. The line ends ca without a clearly printed hyphen.

runs.text: ſa. ¶ Itẽ, A primeira vez que hum vai a

lines.note: Completes casa and gives a further sense: the first time someone goes to a place. The printed verb vai corrects OCR oai, and Itẽ retains its abbreviation mark.

runs.text: algum lugar, reino, ou cidade. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the list of a place, kingdom or city. The example begins V-i and continues as dachi on the next row; no extra terminal hyphen is supplied.
Completes uidachi wo suru, making a first appearance or first visit. The long s in ſuru corrects OCR turu.
Uigo, alternatively uinoko, is the first child born. Vinoco and filho correct the damaged OCR forms Vmnoco and flho.
Uimujo refers back to the ui entry and its explanation of misery and impermanence. The printed j and caron correct the OCR Vimuiǒ.
Uinoko refers back to uigo, the first-born child. The short cross-reference is a complete independent entry.
Uikyo is fennel, directly glossed by funcho. The Japanese long-vowel caron is preserved.
Ui tenben refers to uncertainty and change in life. The printed tenben is retained rather than silently replacing it with a modern tenpen form.

Completes the account of changes in worldly things. Officio at the far right belongs to the following novice-person definition; its opening relocation mark and physical position are preserved explicitly.

runs.text: Peßoa noua ẽ algũa couſa, ou lugar, ou

lines.note: Uiuishii describes someone new to an activity, place or office. The final office is the displaced officio above; the scan visibly separates Vi and vixij, and the attributed NINJAL index corroborates that headword spacing.
Gives related forms uiuishisa and uiuishu, continuing the novice or inexperienced-person entry. The scan does not contain the OCR paragraph mark or Vt; the final vowel bears a caron, not an o.

runs.text: Hũa mezinha como cobra, ou lagartixa ſeca.

lines.note: Uja is described as a medicinal substance like a dried snake or lizard. The visible word is ſeca, dry, rather than OCR ſeua; no more precise identification is imposed.
Ujo is paraphrased as sho aru mono and means a living, sentient thing. The damaged but present final ǒ in the headword corrects OCR Vj.
Sentido completes the preceding living-and-sentient definition. Ujo and hijo then contrast sentient with insentient things; the first word remains part of the Portuguese gloss.
Completes the contrast with insentient things, or things without life and sensation. It belongs to the ujo/hijo pair above.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de laranjas que chamão,

lines.note: Uju is a kind of orange called mikan. Micã is a Japanese name embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is visibly upright; its nasal abbreviation is retained.
Ujukit is offered as the preferable form for the preceding citrus name. Melius and Idem belong to the editorial apparatus; the final t is not expanded into a modern syllable.

runs.text: Interjeição do que conſente, ou entendeo

lines.note: Um is an interjection of assent or understanding. The scan supports initial Interjeição and the printed sequence entendeo; the complement que lhe dizem follows below.
Completes the description as understanding what someone says to the person. The damaged h of lhe is recovered from the surviving stroke and the construction.
Uma means horse. Uma ni noru is riding a horse, with the alternative mesu divided across rows; the damaged headword is Vma, not the OCR Vmna.
Completes mesu, glossed as riding. Uma no tazuna wo begins the next example involving the horse's reins.
Completes tazuna wo kaesu, turning the horse by its reins. Vma- begins the next example; its damaged m is not an n.
Completes uma ga yokodatsu, a horse standing across the way. The Portuguese explanation continues with the location, the path, below.
Completes the horse obstructing the path. Uma wo semuru introduces the exercise or training of a horse.
Completes exercising the horse, then defines seme uma as a horse undergoing such exercise. The relative clause continues on the next row.
Completes exercise by running, then gives uma wo hiyasu, cooling a horse. The scan has long ſ in fiyaſu, not the OCR accented vowel fiyaǔ.
Translates hiyasu as washing and cooling the horse. The next example begins with uma wo and continues below.
Completes uma wo kakuru, making the horse run. Ashi begins the alternative expression ashi wo dasu on the next line.
Completes ashi wo dasu with the same running meaning. The next example begins uma wo kakeawaseru, divided at caqeaua-.
Completes kakeawaseru; the Portuguese describes horsemen lowering or levelling their lances for an encounter. The historical Enraſtarem is preserved.
Uma wo hinmawasu turns the horse by pulling it around. The direction is specified in the next line; ca- is the beginning of caualo.

runs.text: ualo pera aparte, ou mãoeſquerda puxandoo.

lines.note: Completes turning the horse toward the left by pulling. The nasal mark is visibly over the a in mão, correcting the OCR split mã oeſquerda; the close setting mãoeſquerda and both final o letters in puxandoo are retained.
Uma wo tsunmawasu is the corresponding turn toward the other side. The Portuguese begins make it turn toward the direction named below.

Completes the rightward turn, then gives uma wo noru with the meaning to go on horseback. The printed object particle uo is retained even though the earlier example used ni; ca- is continued or anticipated by the isolated bottom-right ualo.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: The isolated bottom-right ualo. is provisionally classified as a catchword anticipating the continuation of ca-. The following page was not supplied, so duplication there could not be directly verified.
